qaPairs.question: What is LoRA? Why is it used for fine-tuning LLMs?
qaPairs.answer:
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that drastically reduces the compute and memory needed to fine-tune large language models. Problem with full fine-tuning: GPT-3 (175B parameters) full fine-tuning requires 8 A100 GPUs + weeks of training. Most companies can't afford this. How LoRA works: Instead of updating ALL model weights, LoRA adds small trainable 'adapter' matrices to each layer. The original model weights are FROZEN. Only the small adapters (< 1% of parameters) are trained. Benefits: • 10-100x less GPU memory required
Training is 3-5x faster
Can fine-tune a 7B model on a single consumer
GPU (RTX 4090)
Multiple LoRA adapters can be swapped for different tasks
Original model unchanged —
easy rollback Variants: QLoRA (Quantized LoRA) = LoRA + 4-bit quantization = even more memory efficient. Used to fine-tune 70B models on a single A100.
Example: LoRA is like adding a small plugin to a large software system rather than rewriting the entire codebase. The core program (LLM) is unchanged — you just add a lightweight extension.
Interview Tip: LoRA knowledge is impressive for freshers. If you mention QLoRA and 4-bit quantization, even better. Shows you follow cutting-edge ML research.

qaPairs.question: What is Transfer Learning? How does it apply to LLMs?
qaPairs.answer:
Transfer Learning is the technique of taking a model pre-trained on a large general dataset and adapting it for a specific task or domain — instead of training from scratch. How it applies to LLMs: 1. Pre-training: Train LLM on massive web text (Common Crawl, Wikipedia, books). Learns language, facts, reasoning. Very expensive ($10M+ for large models). 2. Fine-tuning (Transfer Learning): Take pre-trained LLM → train on your specific domain data. Learns domain-specific style and knowledge. Much cheaper. 3. RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — align LLM with human preferences (helpful, harmless, honest). Why Transfer Learning works: The pre-trained model already knows grammar, world knowledge, reasoning. Fine-tuning teaches it YOUR specific domain on top of this foundation. Analogy: Pre-training = 12 years of school education (general knowledge). Fine-tuning = 2 years of medical school (specific domain).
Example: Google pre-trained BERT on Wikipedia + Books Corpus. Then researchers fine-tuned it for medical Q&A; by training on medical literature. The model kept its language understanding but gained medical expertise.
Interview Tip: Transfer learning is a classic ML concept applied to LLMs. Fresher interviews at traditional IT companies (TCS, Infosys) ask this because it connects ML basics to LLMs. SECTION 6: Production & Evaluation (Q27–Q30)

qaPairs.question: What is RAGAS? How do you evaluate a RAG system?
qaPairs.answer:
RAGAS (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment) is the standard framework for evaluating RAG systems automatically using LLM-as-a-judge. 4 Key RAGAS Metrics: 1. Faithfulness: Is the answer supported by the retrieved context? (Measures hallucination) Target: > 0.90. If low: LLM is adding information not in retrieved docs. 2. Answer Relevancy: Does the answer actually address the question asked? Target: > 0.85. If low: Answer is off-topic. 3. Context Precision: Of the retrieved chunks, what % are actually relevant? Target: > 0.70. If low: Retrieval is returning irrelevant chunks. 4. Context Recall: Were all relevant documents retrieved? Target: > 0.75. If low: Relevant documents are being missed. Simple evaluation process: 1. Create a golden dataset: 50-100 Q&A; pairs with expected answers 2. Run your RAG system on all questions 3. Calculate RAGAS metrics
4. Identify the weakest metric → fix that component 5. Re-evaluate after fixes
Example: RAGAS is like a report card for your RAG system: Faithfulness = accuracy, Relevancy = on-topic %, Precision = retrieval quality, Recall = coverage. All four need to be high for a good system.
Interview Tip: Knowing RAGAS metrics by name and what each measures is impressive for freshers. Most candidates don't go beyond 'I would evaluate accuracy.' RAGAS shows real depth.

qaPairs.question: What is Responsible AI? What are the key principles?
qaPairs.answer:
Responsible AI is the practice of designing, developing, and deploying AI systems that are safe, fair, transparent, and aligned with human values. 6 Key Principles: 1. Fairness: AI should not discriminate. Example: Loan approval AI should not be biased against any gender or race. 2. Reliability & Safety: AI must work correctly and not cause harm. Example: Self-driving car AI must handle edge cases safely. 3. Privacy & Security: Protect user data. AI trained on private data must not leak it. 4. Inclusiveness: AI should work for everyone — different languages, abilities, cultures. 5. Transparency: Users should know they're interacting with AI. Decisions should be explainable. 6. Accountability: Someone is responsible for AI's decisions and errors. Clear ownership. For
GenAI specifically:
Prevent hallucination (accuracy)
Prevent prompt injection attacks (security)
Prevent
generating harmful content (safety)
Cite sources (transparency)
Human-in-the-loop for high-stakes decisions
(accountability)
Example: Amazon's AI recruiting tool (2018) was found biased against women — trained on historical data from male-dominated tech hiring. It was scrapped. This is a real Responsible AI failure.
Interview Tip: Every company now asks about ethics/responsible AI. It's not just technical — it's a values question. Show you think beyond features to impacts. The Amazon example is a famous real case.

qaPairs.question: How do you deploy a GenAI application to production?
qaPairs.answer:
Deploying a GenAI application involves several layers beyond just calling an LLM API: Step 1: Model Layer
Choose: API (OpenAI, Gemini API) vs Self-hosted (Llama on GKE)
For freshers: API is recommended
— no infrastructure management Step 2: Application Layer
FastAPI or Flask backend to handle requests •
LangChain or LlamaIndex for RAG pipeline logic
Docker containerize the application Step 3: Deployment •
Cloud Run (Google): Serverless, auto-scales, easy deployment
Cloud Run command: gcloud run deploy
my-genai-app --image gcr.io/project/app
Or: AWS Lambda, Azure Container Apps Step 4: Production concerns
Rate limiting: Prevent abuse (100 requests/minute per user)
Caching: Cache common responses (Redis) —
saves cost and latency
Monitoring: Log every request, response, latency, token count
Streaming: Stream
tokens to user instead of waiting for full response
• Error handling: Retry on API failures, fallback models Step 5:
Evaluation pipeline
Weekly RAGAS evaluation on golden dataset
Alert if quality metrics drop
Example: Simple architecture: User → FastAPI backend (Cloud Run) → LangChain RAG pipeline → Gemini API + Vertex AI Search → Response streamed back to user.
Interview Tip: For fresher interviews, just knowing the basic architecture (FastAPI + Docker + Cloud Run + LangChain) is enough. Mentioning streaming and caching shows production awareness.

qaPairs.question: What would you build as your first GenAI project to showcase in an interview?
qaPairs.answer:
Best fresher GenAI projects (in order of impressiveness): 1. PDF Chatbot (RAG): Upload any PDF → Ask questions → Get answers with citations. Shows: RAG pipeline, embeddings, vector DB, LangChain. 2. Resume Screening Tool: Upload job description + resumes → AI ranks candidates. Shows: LLM integration, structured output, practical use case. 3. Multi-language FAQ Bot: Company FAQ in English → Users can ask in any language → Gets translated answer. Shows: LLM, prompt engineering, API integration. 4. AI Code Reviewer: Paste code → Get review, bugs identified, improvements suggested. Shows: Prompt engineering, LLM capabilities. 5. YouTube Video Summarizer: Enter YouTube URL → Get structured summary + timestamps. Shows: API integration, prompt engineering, document processing. Minimum tech stack for a good portfolio
project:
Python + LangChain or LlamaIndex
OpenAI API or Google Gemini API (free tier)
ChromaDB for
vector storage (local, free)
Streamlit for quick UI (free)
GitHub for code + README with architecture diagram
Time to build: 1-2 weekends. Cost: $5-10 in API credits.
Example: Build the PDF chatbot first — it covers RAG, embeddings, vector DB, and LLM in one project. Put it on GitHub with a clear README. Demo it live in interviews.
Interview Tip: Having even ONE working GenAI project puts you ahead of 80% of freshers who only have theoretical knowledge. Build something, deploy it, and talk about what you learned from failures.
